_what: Competing explanations for the clustering of extreme trans-Neptunian orbits, each against the two clues (they stretch out and tilt the same way) and what it needs. Drives insights/alternatives.html.
_caution: The assessments below are our summary of the published arguments, not a quantitative ranking. 'status' is editorial.

_fields.explains: what this hypothesis accounts for well
_fields.struggles_with: what it does not account for, per its critics
_fields.key_dois: entries in papers.json: every DOI cited in explain and struggles
_fields.explain: what the idea is and what it explains, in plain words: sentences of {text, cite}, cite = DOIs in papers.json, shown as superscripts that link to the credits page
_fields.struggles: where it falls short, the panel's key line; same shape as explain
_fields.fits: each clue (stretch, tilt): v (yes, times, disputed, fades, unshown, no, chance, apparent), one plain sentence, cite = DOIs; written by scripts/tag_alternatives.py from the papers
_fields.needs: what it asks us to accept that has not been seen: tier (an index into tiers, the map's rows), a sentence, cite
_fields.issue: its main problem, one or two plain sentences and cite: the last line of its card
_fields.gist: a few words on what the idea is, shown on pointing at it on the map

alternatives.name: A ninth planet
alternatives.one_liner: An undiscovered 5-10 Earth-mass planet on a distant, eccentric, anti-aligned orbit shepherds the extreme objects.

explain.text: A planet five to ten times Earth's mass, on a stretched, tilted orbit far beyond Neptune, would slowly pull the distant orbits into line.
The same pull would lift some of them out of Neptune's reach and tip others steeply out of the plane of the planets.

struggles.text: Nobody has found it after a decade of searching,
and surveys that kept careful track of where they looked see the orbits bunch less, or not at all.

alternatives.mechanism: Secular and resonant gravitational interaction over hundreds of millions of years confines the longitudes of perihelion of distant objects anti-aligned to the planet's own.
explains: apsidal clustering of the extreme objects
detached objects like Sedna with perihelia beyond Neptune's reach
struggles_with: nobody has found it, despite a decade of targeted searching
the clustering signal weakens when only bias-characterised surveys are used

stretch.text: A planet's pull would keep the distant orbits stretched out opposite to the planet's orbit, for billions of years.

tilt.text: The same pull would tilt the orbits the same way as the planet's orbit.

needs.text: A planet several times Earth's mass, hundreds of AU out, not yet found.

issue.text: No search has found the planet yet.

alternatives.gist: An unseen planet far beyond Neptune.

alternatives.name: Luck
alternatives.tag: too few orbits to be sure
alternatives.one_liner: With only a handful of well-determined extreme orbits, an apparent alignment can simply be luck.

explain.text: The case began with just six distant objects, and the set with well-known orbits is still small.
In a small set, a few orbits lining up by chance is not unusual, as shuffling the sky on the last page shows.

struggles.text: As more objects have been found, Brown and Batygin still find the bunching unlikely to be chance.

alternatives.mechanism: Not a physical mechanism. The original claim rested on six objects, and the human eye finds patterns in small samples readily.
explains: why the significance has shifted as objects were added and removed from the sample
struggles_with: the sample has grown and the proponents' significance estimates have not collapsed

stretch.text: In {p_stretch} of random samples of known objects, the orbits stretch out as tightly as today's.

tilt.text: In {p_tilt} of the samples, the orbits tilt as tightly.

needs.text: Nothing new, only luck. About 1 in {odds} samples are as tight in both.

issue.text: Both together happen in only about 1 in {odds} samples (though studies of other surveys find the pattern far less unusual).

alternatives.gist: The orbits line up by chance.

alternatives.name: Where telescopes looked
alternatives.one_liner: There is no real clustering. Telescopes searched particular patches of sky at particular times of year, and that alone shapes which orbits get found.

explain.text: Distant objects are faint, so we mostly spot them when they swing closest to the Sun, and only where telescopes happen to point.
If the searches looked more in some directions, the objects found would seem to stretch out that way, even if the real ones stretch out every way.
Surveys that kept careful track of where they looked find no clear bunching among their own objects.

struggles.text: Allowing for where telescopes looked, Brown and Batygin still find only about a 1 in 500 chance of bunching this strong.

alternatives.mechanism: Distant objects are only detectable near perihelion. Survey pointings cluster around the ecliptic, around good observing seasons and away from the galactic plane, so the discovered sample inherits that pattern.
explains: why the apparent clustering is strongest in heterogeneously discovered samples
why OSSOS and DES, which model their own detection efficiency, see a much weaker signal
struggles_with: Brown & Batygin's bias-corrected analyses still find the clustering significant at roughly 1 in 500
does not obviously explain the high-inclination population
alternatives.sketch_cue: survey footprint overlay on the sky map

stretch.text: Telescopes find distant objects mostly where they happen to look, so the objects found could seem to stretch out one way even if the real ones do not.

tilt.text: The same could make the orbits seem to tilt one way. Surveys that tracked where they pointed find no clear sign of either.

needs.text: Allowing for where telescopes looked, Brown and Batygin still find only a 0.2% chance of clustering this strong.

issue.text: Allowing for where telescopes looked, Brown and Batygin still put the chance of clustering this strong at 0.2%.

alternatives.gist: Telescopes found only the objects where they looked.

alternatives.name: A passing star
alternatives.one_liner: A close stellar encounter, in the Sun's birth cluster or more recently, sculpted the distant orbits and then left.

explain.text: While the Sun was still among the stars it formed with, one of them may have passed close enough to pull distant orbits away from Neptune.
One strong pass like that could also leave the orbits stretching out one way.
One recent simulation, a star a little smaller than the Sun passing about 110 AU away, also reproduces the steeply tilted orbits, even those that run backwards.

struggles.text: Left alone afterwards, the giant planets would spread the orbits out again in far less time than the age of the solar system.

alternatives.mechanism: A single impulsive encounter can lift perihelia and imprint a preferred orbital orientation that survives for a long time afterwards.
struggles_with: the imprint should disperse over billions of years
explains the existence of detached objects better than it explains present-day clustering
alternatives.note: Widely discussed as an origin for Sedna-like orbits; less favoured as the sole cause of the current clustering.

stretch.text: A star passing the young Sun could have lifted orbits like Sedna's, but no study shows the star lining the orbits up.

tilt.text: No study shows the star lining up the tilt either.

needs.text: Nothing new. The Sun formed among other stars, and one may have passed within about 110 AU.

issue.text: With nothing to hold it in place, any pattern would fade within a few hundred million years.

alternatives.gist: A star that passed close to the young Sun.

alternatives.name: A heavy disk of small bodies
alternatives.one_liner: A few Earth masses of small bodies spread through the distant belt can confine each other's orbits, with no single planet required.

explain.text: Instead of one planet, a wide, lopsided ring of many small icy bodies could hold the orbits in line with their combined pull.
It can bunch the orbits and keep them away from Neptune, with no planet needed.

struggles.text: It needs about ten Earth masses of material out there, where standard estimates allow only a few tenths of one.

alternatives.mechanism: Collective secular gravity of a massive disk of planetesimals drives apsidal confinement of embedded orbits.
struggles_with: requires far more mass in the outer belt than current estimates allow
does not naturally produce the perpendicular objects
alternatives.sketch_cue: ring of many small bodies, no planet

stretch.text: A lopsided ring of small icy bodies could hold the orbits stretched out opposite to the ring.

tilt.text: In the same simulations, the orbits still tilt every way.

needs.text: About 10 Earth masses of small bodies, but estimates allow only a few tenths.

issue.text: The ring would need about 10 Earth masses, but estimates allow only a few tenths.

alternatives.gist: A heavy, lopsided ring of small icy bodies.

alternatives.name: A self-tilting swarm
alternatives.one_liner: A sufficiently massive population of eccentric distant bodies spontaneously lifts and aligns itself out of the plane.

explain.text: If the distant bodies together weigh enough, their own pull can tip the whole swarm out of the plane of the planets and lift it away from Neptune.
Later, in idealised computer models, the orbits also stretch out one way for a while.

struggles.text: It needs about twenty Earth masses of small bodies far out to get started,
far more than anyone thinks is there.

alternatives.mechanism: A collective dynamical instability in a disk of high-eccentricity orbits raises inclinations and clusters arguments of perihelion, and later apsidal angles as well.
struggles_with: needs roughly an Earth mass or more of material in the extreme population, which may not exist

stretch.text: Enough distant objects could pull one another out of the planets' plane. In simplified simulations, the orbits then stretch out one way.

tilt.text: No study shows the orbits tilting the same way.

needs.text: About 20 Earth masses of small bodies far out.

issue.text: The swarm would need the mass of about twenty Earths, much more than estimates allow. Simulations also showed that the clustering did not last.

alternatives.gist: Distant objects that pull one another out of the plane.

alternatives.name: Modified gravity
alternatives.tag: different rules far from the Sun
alternatives.one_liner: Gravity itself departs from Newton at the very low accelerations found hundreds of AU out.

explain.text: Far from the Sun, where its pull is extremely weak, gravity itself might not follow Newton's law.
One such law, proposed to explain how galaxies spin, would bunch the distant orbits with no extra body to find.

struggles.text: But Saturn's orbit, measured very precisely, shows no extra pull,
and in simulations over the Sun's lifetime it fails to reproduce the comets that fall in from the far edge of the solar system, or the orbits cut off from Neptune.

alternatives.mechanism: MOND-like external field effects would alter orbital precession rates in the outer solar system without any extra mass.
struggles_with: planetary ephemerides constrain deviations from Newtonian gravity very tightly inside Saturn's orbit
simulated over the Sun's lifetime, the popular AQUAL form fails to reproduce long-period comets and the detached disk
alternatives.sketch_cue: warped grid instead of a mass

stretch.text: If gravity worked differently far from the Sun, one version would stretch the orbits out towards the centre of the Galaxy. More detailed simulations found no lining up.

tilt.text: That version would leave the orbits tilting every way.

needs.text: A change to gravity far from the Sun.

issue.text: If gravity changed far from the Sun, the planets would move slightly differently too. Precise tracking of Saturn shows no such change, as the idea's own authors note.

alternatives.gist: Gravity that works differently far from the Sun.

alternatives.name: A primordial black hole
alternatives.tag: a planet's mass, no bigger than a bowling ball
alternatives.one_liner: The perturber is real, but it is a grapefruit-sized black hole of the same mass rather than a planet.

explain.text: The unseen body could be a black hole left over from the early universe, with a planet's mass but no bigger than a bowling ball.
Its pull would match a planet's, so it explains everything a planet does, and telescopes looking for reflected sunlight would never see it.

struggles.text: Such black holes would have to exist and the Sun would have to have captured one, and it could be confirmed only indirectly.

alternatives.mechanism: Identical gravity, so identical dynamics. It would be invisible to reflected-light searches and detectable only through accretion flares, lensing, or occultations.
explains: why optical surveys have not found it
struggles_with: requires capture of a primordial black hole, which is speculative
no detection in dedicated searches so far
alternatives.sketch_cue: black dot where the planet would be

stretch.text: Planet Nine could be a black hole from the early universe, with a planet's mass but no bigger than a bowling ball. The black hole's pull would stretch the orbits out just as a planet's would.

tilt.text: The orbits would tilt the same way too.

needs.text: A kind of black hole never seen, left over from the early universe and captured by the Sun. It would be no bigger than a bowling ball and reflect no sunlight.

issue.text: Black holes this small are still hypothetical, and none has ever been confirmed. A black hole would also reflect no sunlight, so a search for a planet would never see one.

alternatives.gist: Planet Nine as a black hole from the early universe.
